newsitem.title: THAILAND: Insurance firms see poll as key to new licences.
newsitem.headline: Insurance firms see poll as key to new licences.

text.p: Foreign insurance firms eyeing Thailand are closely monitoring political changes in this major Southeast Asian market to see if a new government after November 17 polls will speed up plans to grant new licences.
The plan to issue 66 new life and non-life licences is the first of three phases in the full liberalisation of a 101 billion baht (US$4 billion) market that grew 20 percent last year.

Thailand's controversial licensing process has been stalled for the past seven months awaiting cabinet approval. Now, it is set to be further delayed after Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa dissolved his coalition government and called snap elections last Friday.
"I think they've been a bit put off," said Michael Huddart, chief financial officer of Ayudhya Jardine CMG Life Assurance, referring to members of the insurance industry.
"There are quite a few foreign (insurance) companies keen to come to Thailand."
He said foreign companies, including Australia's National Mutual, had scaled down plans to expand in Thailand because of the delay.
Surachai Sirivallop, head of Thai Reinsurance Company, said the licensing snag was symptomatic of a lack of a coherent government policy towards the industry.

"How can this industry develop in such an environment? There is never any serious planning or continuity. This has gone on for years and years. It is a big mistake not to look at this seriously," he said.

Foreign companies are permitted to hold only 25 percent stakes in newly licensed insurers, although consideration has been made to increase this to 49 percent after the new firms start operating, leading to full foreign ownership in about a decade.
Current insurers in Thailand oppose the planned licensing of 66 new rivals because it would almost double the number of players in the market.
Nigel Smith, general manager of Sun Alliance (Thailand), said margins had been hit by the plan.

"Things are very competitive at the moment. When it was announced that 66 companies might be approved, there's widespread panic as people try to increase market shares. Rates took a significant tumble, premiums dropped 40-50 percent on some lines," Smith said.
He said if 66 new licences were granted, a severe staff shortage would hit the industry.
Current insurers hoped to see the number of new licensees reduced. "I think everyone would be reasonably happy if the licences are issued at a slower pace," said Huddart.

Despite tougher times ahead, long-term rewards are waiting for those who can wait. Only 10 percent of Thailand's increasingly affluent 60 million people take out life insurance policies in a market worth 48 billion baht in 1995.

Thailand's corporate life insurance sector lies virtually untouched, while Thais' addiction to cars provided 60 percent of annual premiums in the 53 billion baht, non-life market in a largely catastrophe free country.
Some big Thai firms, including Shinawatra, Alphatec and Charoen Pokphand Group, are keen to enter the market. (US$1 = 25 baht)
